turns:
=== CALL C0163 ===
Craig: Hiya, can you hear me alright?
Lorraine A: Yeah. Yeah, I can hear you.
Craig: Brilliant. I'm Craig, I'm up in Lancaster. Where are you, mate? Sorry, not mate, er, force of habit.
Lorraine A: It's alright. Lorraine. Wednesbury, near Walsall.
Craig: Oh right, Black Country. I've been through on the M6 loads, never actually stopped, which is probably an insult, sorry.
Lorraine A: Nobody stops. Don't worry about it.
Craig: Fair enough. Did you do that puzzle at the start? I was rubbish. I kept going back and changing them.
Lorraine A: Erm, I did it. I don't know if I did it right. I don't see what it's got to do with anything, to be honest.
Craig: No, me neither. I think they just want to see if you panic.
Lorraine A: Well I did. So.
Craig: Join the club. So are you working at the minute?
Lorraine A: Not at the minute, no. I was a machinist. Upholstery, cushion covers, curtains, that sort of thing, at a place in Darlaston. It shut about eighteen months ago. So I've been sort of... doing these, and walking the dog, you know.
Craig: Ah, that's rough. Were you there long?
Lorraine A: Long enough. I liked it. You just got on with it, nobody bothered you as long as your seams were straight. ...Anyway.
Craig: That sounds like the dream, honestly. I manage a bike shop, so I've got four staff and they're bothering me all day. Well, not bothering. Asking stuff. I'd rather be in the workshop building a wheel, you know, than doing rotas.
Lorraine A: I saw the bike. In your picture. In the house.
Craig: Yeah, that's Nadia's favourite thing, the bike in the front room. My partner. She's given up. There's another one in the hall, to be fair.
Lorraine A: I'd go mad. Our Kieran leaves his football boots on the stairs and I'm at him every day about it.
Craig: How old's Kieran?
Lorraine A: Fifteen. Year ten. So he doesn't listen to anything.
Craig: I was exactly the same at fifteen, my mum'll tell you. Is that your dog in the photo as well? I could see a bit of a head.
Lorraine A: Bella. Staffie cross. She's on the settee now, she's... oh, hang on, she's looking at the door. She'll want letting out. Sorry.
Craig: No, go for it, honestly.
Lorraine A: No, she can wait. She does this.
Craig: So do you still sew, like at home?
Lorraine A: Erm, yeah. I've got me old Singer. I do bits for people. Taking trousers up, me mum's curtains. People keep saying I should charge, but you'd have to set it all up, wouldn't you, and I'm no good with all that. Forms and that.
Craig: I'm the same with the shop's books, I leave it till the last day. But alterations, people round us can't find anyone. There's a woman two streets over and she's booked up for weeks. If you're fast, you'd be fine.
Lorraine A: I am fast. I'll give you that.
Craig: There you go then.
Lorraine A: Mm. It's all very well, though, isn't it. It's the money for the first bit. With the electric what it is.
Craig: Yeah, no, fair. It's not nothing.
Lorraine A: What do you do Sundays then, ride the bike?
Craig: Yeah, long ride, out to the Trough of Bowland usually, then a bacon barm and a pint after. That's basically my whole personality.
Lorraine A: A what?
Craig: A barm. Bread roll. Barm cake.
Lorraine A: It's a bap.
Craig: It's a barm, Lorraine.
Lorraine A: It's a bap. Bacon bap, Saturday morning, every week. Gary does it.
Craig: Right, I'll give you Saturday, but I'm not budging on the —

=== CALL C0164 ===
Colin: Hello there. Is that, er, is that working? Can you see me?
Lorraine B: Yes, I can see you. Hiya. Sorry, I've got the sound up now.
Colin: Lovely. I'm Colin. I'm in Worthing, down on the south coast.
Lorraine B: Lorraine. I'm near Wrexham. Rhos, Rhosllannerchrugog, but nobody can say it, so I just say Wrexham.
Colin: Rhos... no, I'm not even going to try, I'll embarrass myself. Wrexham I know, though. That's the football lot, isn't it, with the film stars.
Lorraine B: That's it. You can't move in town on a match day now. It's lovely for them, mind.
Colin: I bet. Did you get on alright with the puzzle at the start?
Lorraine B: Erm, sort of. I do word searches, so I thought I'd be alright, but it wasn't really like that, was it.
Colin: No. I did about half and then my brain went for a walk. My wife does the crossword with me and she normally carries me, so on my own I was a bit lost.
Lorraine B: Oh dear.
Colin: So what do you do with yourself, Lorraine? Are you working?
Lorraine B: Not at the minute. I was at the college in Wrexham. I ran the morning cleaning team there for a good few years. Then the contract changed hands and they offered voluntary redundancy, so I took it. I'm looking for something part-time now, a school kitchen maybe, or a care home. Just daytimes. Sorry, I'm waffling.
Colin: You're not waffling at all. Running a team at half five in the morning, that's no joke.
Lorraine B: Half five, yes. You get used to it. It's getting un-used to it that's funny.
Colin: I know just what you mean. I was a joiner, forty-odd years, and when I packed it in I kept waking at six thinking I'd got a kitchen to fit. Took me a year to stop.
Lorraine B: Did it? That's good to know, actually.
Colin: Oh yes. Now I just potter. I've got a shed, do a bit of woodturning, bowls and that. I've got one on the go out of a bit of old cherry. It's come out a bit lopsided, but I'm telling everyone it's deliberate.
Lorraine B: I saw a little bowl on your shelf, in the picture. Was that one of yours?
Colin: That was, yes. One of the better ones. The bad ones go to the family. No, that's not true. Well, it's a bit true.
Lorraine B: My grandson would love one. He's into dinosaurs at the minute, everything's dinosaurs. He'd want a T-rex on it.
Colin: How old is he?
Lorraine B: Five. He's in Mold with my daughter. I have him most weekends.
Colin: Oh, that's lovely. We've got two in Brighton, we pick them up from school on a Wednesday. Ours were dinosaurs, then it was space, now it's some cartoon I can't keep up with.
Lorraine B: That's what's coming, then.
Colin: That's what's coming. Do you get out much yourself, walking or anything?
Lorraine B: Every day if I can. Up round the lanes, or along Ponciau Banks. My knee doesn't like the hill, but I go anyway.
Colin: Good for you. I'm on the Downs most days. Got absolutely soaked up there last week, came home like a drowned rat and Maureen wouldn't let me in the kitchen. Anyway, where was I. Oh, walking. My dad didn't make sixty, so I sort of think, keep moving, you know.
Lorraine B: Oh, I'm sorry. My mam went three years ago. You do think about it, don't you.
Colin: You do. Sorry to hear that, love.
Lorraine B: Thank you. I don't know if that's what... anyway. What are you having for tea tonight?
Colin: For dinner? Oh, I've no idea, Maureen's in charge. Probably something sensible. I did a paella once and we've not —

=== CALL C0165 ===
Craig: Hiya, can you hear me alright?
Tomasz: Yes. Hello. Yeah, I can hear you.
Craig: Champion. I'm Craig, I'm in Lancaster.
Tomasz: Tomasz. I'm in Exeter.
Craig: Exeter, nice. Long way down. I clocked the Dartmoor map in your picture. Do you get up there much?
Tomasz: Erm, yeah. Quite a lot. Most weekends, if I'm not on shift.
Craig: On shift where, if you don't mind me asking?
Tomasz: Food factory, on the edge of Exeter. I'm machine operator on a packing line. And I'm also student, sorry, I mean I'm a student as well. Archaeology. Second year.
Craig: Both at once? That must be knackering.
Tomasz: It is, yeah. Last week one machine kept jamming all night, I got home at six and had seminar at ten. So.
Craig: Oof. Did you make it?
Tomasz: I made it. I didn't say anything, but I made it.
Craig: Fair play. I tried uni, actually. Outdoor education, up in Cumbria. Lasted a year, then I couldn't afford it and I just sort of felt like I didn't fit, you know. Went and fixed bikes instead.
Tomasz: Mm. I did one year of history in Poland. Then I left, came here. And now I'm back at thirty-seven, oldest one in the room. The students are very nice to me. Like I'm their uncle.
Craig: Ha, that's not a bad position to be in, to be fair. So when you're up on Dartmoor, are you just walking, or is it, like, for the course?
Tomasz: Bit of both. Erm, Dartmoor is full of Bronze Age stuff, if you know where to look. Stone rows, long lines of stones going across the moor, sometimes hundreds of metres, and nobody really knows why. And hut circles, where people lived, you can still see the rings of the walls in the grass. And the old field boundaries, reaves, they cut right across the moor. When you understand what you're looking at, it's like the whole landscape is sort of a document. Most people walk past. I don't blame them, it's raining usually.
Craig: Stone rows, yeah. That's brilliant, actually. We ride past Castlerigg sometimes, up near Keswick, the stone circle, and I always think I should stop and actually look at it instead of just stopping for a flapjack.
Tomasz: Castlerigg I want to see. People say it's the best setting, with the mountains round it.
Craig: It is, honestly. You should come up. Bring the wife, do the Lakes.
Tomasz: Hannah would like that. She likes when I plan something. I don't plan, usually.
Craig: I'm the opposite, I plan routes for fun. Nadia thinks it's a sickness.
Tomasz: Maybe it is. But useful sickness.
Craig: I'll take that. What else are you into, apart from rocks?
Tomasz: Books. Too many at once. History, and Polish science fiction, Lem mostly.
Craig: No way, I've got Solaris on the shelf. I've been reading loads of sci-fi lately. Haven't started that one, though, it looked a bit heavy.
Tomasz: Solaris is heavy, yeah. Start with The Cyberiad. It's robots building machines that do stupid things. It's very funny. Then Solaris, when you're ready to be sad.
Craig: Ready to be sad, right. Noted. Are you reading something for uni at the minute or is that all Lem?
Tomasz: I should be reading for an essay. Bronze Age burial practices. I'm behind. It's due Friday, so I'll do it Thursday night, like always.
Craig: Thursday night, classic. Is that the cairns and that, or —
Tomasz: Cairns, cists, barrows. There's a cist on Dartmoor, at Whitehorse Hill, they found a burial with beads and a basket, and the —

=== CALL C0166 ===
Colin: Hello there. Colin, down in Worthing. Can you hear me alright?
Lorraine A: Yeah. Lorraine. Wednesbury.
Colin: Black Country. I had a mate from Dudley years ago, a plasterer. Lovely bloke, couldn't understand a word he said.
Lorraine A: Well, we're not all like that.
Colin: No, he was quite extreme. Saw your dog in the picture, I think. Just the top of her head.
Lorraine A: Bella. She's here now. She's twelve, she's going a bit grey round the face.
Colin: Ah, bless her. We lost ours, ooh, three years back. I'd have another tomorrow but Maureen's not keen, so I just sort of make a fuss of everyone else's.
Lorraine A: She's hard work. Canal every morning, rain or not. She don't care.
Colin: That's the best thing about them, though, isn't it, they get you out. I do the Downs, or the seafront. What do you do when you're not walking her? Working?
Lorraine A: Not at the minute. I was a machinist, upholstery, till the firm shut. I've said this already once today, I feel like a record.
Colin: Ha, I know, I was a joiner, I've said that twice. Funny, I used to work with upholsterers. I'd build a window seat and then the upholstery lady'd come and do the cushions, and she'd tell me off if my measurements were out.
Lorraine A: Well, they would be, wouldn't they. That's what we was always saying. The frames come in wrong and we've got to make it fit.
Colin: Guilty. I was probably the one sending them in wrong.
Lorraine A: Probably.
Colin: Do you still sew at all?
Lorraine A: Bits. Alterations, for family. The lad I just spoke to said I should do it proper, charge people. They all say that.
Colin: Well, he's not wrong, but I'll be honest with you, the sewing's the easy bit for you, I should think. It's the rest of it. I was self-employed forty-odd years and my invoices were a shoebox job. Maureen did all my books. I'd have gone under without her and I don't think I ever told her that properly.
Lorraine A: That's it, though. The forms and that. Gary can't do his own tax disc, never mind.
Colin: Find yourself a Maureen. Or a library, they do little business sessions sometimes. Mine did.
Lorraine A: Mm. Maybe. ...It's just you put money in and it all goes wrong, and then where are you. With everything the price it is.
Colin: No, I know. That's a fair worry. You start small, though, don't you. Word of mouth. I never advertised once.
Lorraine A: Did you not?
Colin: Never. People just told people. Anyway, I've gone on. What did you have for dinner last night, go on, something nice.
Lorraine A: Tea. Shepherd's pie.
Colin: Tea, sorry, there you go. Lovely.
Lorraine A: That other lad called a roll a barm. I told him it's a bap.
Colin: Down here it's just a roll, I'm afraid. Boring lot, we are.
Lorraine A: Roll's alright. Barm's daft.
Colin: I'll not tell him you said that. Do you make yours with lamb or is it —

=== CALL C0167 ===
Lorraine B: Hiya. Can you hear me okay?
Tomasz: Yes. Hello. I'm Tomasz.
Lorraine B: Lorraine. I'm near Wrexham. Have you had a busy day?
Tomasz: Erm, not too bad. I was on shift last night, so I'm a bit slow. Sorry if I'm slow.
Lorraine B: Oh, don't be daft. What do you do?
Tomasz: Packing line, food factory. And I'm a student, archaeology, at Exeter. Second year.
Lorraine B: Oh, I thought you looked like a student, with the books. You reminded me of my son, actually. Sorry, that sounds awful.
Tomasz: No, it's fine. I'm thirty-seven, I'm not offended to look young.
Lorraine B: Thirty-seven and doing a degree, good for you. I couldn't. I'd be terrified.
Tomasz: I was terrified. I'm still, sometimes. Everyone is nineteen.
Lorraine B: Well. I don't know if that's... sorry, go on.
Tomasz: No, it's alright. What do you do?
Lorraine B: Nothing at the minute. I ran the cleaning team at the college, mornings, then took redundancy. Looking for something part-time. It's knocked me a bit, if I'm honest, starting again at my age.
Tomasz: Mm. Yeah. I know this feeling.
Lorraine B: You do, don't you, with the uni.
Tomasz: My wife is pharmacist at the hospital. When I saw your picture I thought you look like the ladies she works with. The nice ones. That's a compliment.
Lorraine B: Oh, thanks, love. I'll take that.
Tomasz: Wrexham, erm. Isn't Offa's Dyke near you?
Lorraine B: It is, yes. It goes past Ruabon, not far. I've walked bits of it. It's just a big bank, really, isn't it.
Tomasz: Just a big bank, yes, but think about it. Eighth century, a king in Mercia decides to dig a line from nearly one sea to the other, by hand, with no machines. Thousands of people, shovels, baskets. And there's another one near you, Wat's Dyke, older maybe, and people still argue about who built which and why. So when you walk on it you're standing on something somebody was told to build twelve hundred years ago. I find that... I don't know. Amazing. Sorry. I talk too much about dirt.
Lorraine B: No, I didn't know any of that. I'll look at it different now.
Tomasz: Do you walk a lot?
Lorraine B: Most days. Ponciau Banks, round the lanes. That's all old coal tips, the Banks. My grandad was at Hafod colliery.
Tomasz: Really? That's archaeology too. Industrial. Somebody will dig your grandad's pit one day and write an essay.
Lorraine B: Oh, he'd laugh at that. He'd say they want their heads looking at.
Tomasz: Probably they do.
Lorraine B: Do you get home much? You said, Poland, was it?
Tomasz: Lublin. Once or twice a year. I ring my mum every Sunday.
Lorraine B: That's nice. You keep doing that. I lost my mam three years ago, and I still pick the phone up sometimes to ring her. Silly, isn't it.
Tomasz: No. It's not silly.
Lorraine B: I don't know why I said that. Sorry.
Tomasz: It's fine. Really. What did she — 

=== CALL C0168 ===
Craig: Hiya mate, can you hear me?
Colin: Loud and clear. Colin, Worthing. You must be the barm man.
Craig: Ha! Has Lorraine been talking about me?
Colin: She has. She thinks barm's daft. I said I'd not tell you, so I've told you straight away.
Craig: She was dead set on bap. I respect it. I'm Craig, Lancaster. Your photo, honestly, you look like my dad. That's a good thing.
Colin: I'll take it. I see you've got a bike in the front room. Maureen'd have that out the door.
Craig: Nadia's given up. I run a bike shop, so it's sort of an occupational hazard. I do up old bikes on the side as well, sell them on or give them to the lads at the youth club round the corner.
Colin: Oh, do you now. That's interesting, that. I've been meaning, for about two years, mind, to do some woodwork teaching. Men's shed or a youth project. I was a joiner, see, forty-odd years. Took a couple of apprentices on, and honestly that was the best bit of the whole job, showing a young lad how to cut a joint properly and seeing him get it. One of them still sends me a Christmas card. He had a rough patch with the drink a while back and I kept an eye on him, and he's doing alright now. So I sort of think, I've got all this in my hands and it's sitting in a shed.
Craig: You should, mate. Seriously. Teaching a kid to fix a puncture, they're made up for a week.
Colin: Same principle, isn't it. Your hands do something and it works.
Craig: That's the dream for me, actually. Long-term I want a little workshop-café. Fix bikes in the back, coffee in the front, maybe a bench where people can learn to do their own.
Colin: Now that I'd come to. Would you have a cake?
Craig: Obviously. Non-negotiable. Do you still do woodwork, then?
Colin: Turning, mostly. Bowls. I've got one on now out of old cherry, it's gone a bit lopsided.
Craig: Character.
Colin: That's what I said! Where do you go on holiday, then, you look like you get about.
Craig: Pyrenees on the bike, Lisbon last year. I really want to do Japan before I'm forty.
Colin: Japan! Me too. Before the knees go. It's the temples I want to see, the old wooden ones, they're put together without a nail, some of them. Joints you wouldn't believe.
Craig: No nails, really?
Colin: Hardly any. Hundreds of years standing. I'd just stand there with my mouth open.
Craig: We should go together, honestly. I'll plan it, you can explain the beams.
Colin: Deal. Is your dad a joiner, then, if I look like him?
Craig: Forklift, at the truck plant in Leyland. He's not been brilliant lately, health-wise. I'm trying to get over more.
Colin: You do that. My dad went at fifty-eight. You don't think you'll miss the ordinary stuff, but you —

=== CALL C0169 ===
Colin: Hello, mate. Colin, down in Worthing. Can you hear me alright?
Tomasz: Yes. Hello, Colin. Tomasz, in Exeter.
Colin: Tomasz. Have I said that right?
Tomasz: Yes, perfect. Better than most people.
Colin: I did a bit of Spanish at evening class, so I'm very careful with names now. I saw your Dartmoor map in the picture. I put down you looked like a teacher.
Tomasz: Erm, no. Student. Archaeology, second year. And I work on a packing line, in a factory, nights and weekends.
Colin: Archaeology! Oh, I'm jealous now. I left school at sixteen, did my apprenticeship, never looked back. Except I did, later on. In lockdown I did an online course on the history of architecture, and I loved it more than anything I'd done in years. I thought, why didn't I do this at twenty?
Tomasz: I'm doing it at thirty-seven, so. Maybe it's never too late. Or maybe it is, I'll tell you in two years.
Colin: Ha. What got you into it, then?
Tomasz: Erm, it's a long answer. In Lublin there's the old town and a castle on the hill, and my grandmother used to take me round and tell me who was killed where, which for a child is very exciting. I started history at university there, then I left, came here for factory work, and I thought, okay, that's finished. Fifteen years. Then Hannah, my wife, she sort of pushed me to do the Access course at the college. And now I'm here.
Colin: That's not a long answer, that's a good answer.
Tomasz: Thank you. You were a builder?
Colin: Joiner. Kitchens, staircases, doors. My favourite was old sash windows, though, restoring them. You open one up and you can see how some bloke did it in eighteen-ninety, and he did it better than me, usually.
Tomasz: That's archaeology too, a bit. Reading a building.
Colin: Is it? I'll put it on my CV.
Tomasz: Really. In old buildings they look at how the timber was cut, the tool marks, and it helps to date it.
Colin: Tool marks, yeah. I did a job on a church roof once, years ago, and you could see the adze marks on the beams, every one a bit different. Somebody's whole week, that beam.
Tomasz: Mm. Somebody's whole life, maybe, that roof.
Colin: That's it. That's why I want to see Japan, the old wooden temples. Before the knees go.
Tomasz: Hannah wants Crete. Knossos. I want it too, but she wants the beach as well.
Colin: Oh, you can do both. We did Granada, the Alhambra. I've never seen anything like it. All that carved plaster, it's like lace.
Tomasz: When were you there?
Colin: Ooh, er, let me think. Twenty-twelve? Thirteen? Not the most organised with dates. We missed the train back to Málaga, I remember that.
Tomasz: I don't plan either. I book everything last minute. Hannah gets very angry.
Colin: Maureen too. Thirty-odd years she's been angry, and I've still not learnt.
Tomasz: Good. So there's no hope for me. That's relaxing.
Colin: Ha, none at all, mate. What are you reading at the minute, apart from all the uni stuff?
Tomasz: Lem, again. Polish science fiction. And a book about old field boundaries, which sounds boring, but it's not.
Colin: I'd read that. I've got three library books on the go and I'll finish one, if I'm lucky.
Tomasz: I have four. I think the library is worried about me.
Colin: They'll send someone round. What's the field boundary one, is it —

=== EVENT C0169 ===
{"turn": 18, "line_text": "Mm. Somebody's whole life, maybe, that roof.", "who": "Tomasz", "what": "At the right edge of the frame a T-shirt slips off the clothes airer behind Tomasz and drops out of view to the floor, with a faint soft thump on the mic; Tomasz doesn't turn round."}

=== CALL C0170 ===
Lorraine B: Hiya. Can you hear me okay?
Lorraine A: Yeah. You're Lorraine as well, aren't you. I saw the name.
Lorraine B: I am, yes! I thought that was funny. Wrexham, near enough.
Lorraine A: Wednesbury. Black Country.
Lorraine B: Oh, not too far, then. Are you alright? You look a bit fed up, sorry.
Lorraine A: No, I'm alright. It's just been a lot of talking. I'm not used to it.
Lorraine B: No, me neither. I'm usually stood in my kitchen talking to the radio.
Lorraine A: I liked your kitchen, in your picture. It's like mine. I've got the same bread bin, I think.
Lorraine B: The cream one? From B&M?
Lorraine A: Yeah.
Lorraine B: There you go, then. Are you working, love?
Lorraine A: No. I was a machinist, till the firm shut. Eighteen months now.
Lorraine B: Oh, I'm the same, sort of. I took redundancy from the college last year. I'm looking at school kitchens and that now.
Lorraine A: I applied for a school kitchen. Never heard nothing back.
Lorraine B: They don't, do they. You fill in all them pages and then nothing. It knocks you a bit.
Lorraine A: It does. I hate the forms. And the interview, sitting there with someone half your age asking where you see yourself in five years. I don't know. On me settee.
Lorraine B: That's what I'd say! I'd never dare, mind.
Lorraine A: I would. That's probably why they don't ring.
Lorraine B: Have you got kids?
Lorraine A: One. Kieran, fifteen. He's on his phone all hours, I don't know who he's talking to. It worries me sick, if I'm honest.
Lorraine B: Oh, they're all like it. My son was the same at that age, and he's lovely now. Lives in Chester with his partner. You'd not believe it was the same lad.
Lorraine A: Hope so. Do you go away at all? Holidays?
Lorraine B: Caravan, mostly. Talacre, or Abersoch if we're feeling posh.
Lorraine A: We do Prestatyn! That's next to Talacre, isn't it?
Lorraine B: Right next door. We've probably been in the same chippy.
Lorraine A: Probably. Gary likes the one on the front. I don't like flying, so.
Lorraine B: No, I'm the same. I went to Majorca with my sister twice and I held her hand the whole way.
Lorraine A: I don't talk to mine.
Lorraine B: Oh. I'm sorry, love.
Lorraine A: It's alright. Long story. ...Did you see Corrie last night?
Lorraine B: I did, yes. I couldn't believe it when she —

=== CALL C0171 ===
Tomasz: Hello. Can you hear me?
Lorraine A: Yeah. Lorraine. Wednesbury.
Tomasz: Tomasz. Exeter. You're the last one for me, I think.
Lorraine A: Me too. Thank God. Sorry. Not you. Just all of it.
Tomasz: No, I understand. It's a lot of talking for one day. I don't talk this much in a week.
Lorraine A: You don't look like you'd be quiet. With all them books.
Tomasz: The books are quiet. That's why I like them.
Lorraine A: Fair enough. What do you do, then? You a teacher?
Tomasz: Everybody says teacher. No. Student, archaeology. And I work on a packing line in a food factory, evenings and weekends. Machine operator.
Lorraine A: Oh, right. I was on machines. Sewing machines, industrial. Upholstery. Till it shut.
Tomasz: So you know. When it's going well, nobody talks to you, and you just listen to the machine.
Lorraine A: That's it. That's exactly it. You can hear when something's not right before it goes.
Tomasz: Yes! Last week my machine was jamming all night, and I knew from the sound, before the alarm. The engineer didn't believe me. Then it jammed. Erm, I cleared it myself in the end. I'm the one who does that.
Lorraine A: Bet they don't pay you for it.
Tomasz: No. They don't.
Lorraine A: They never do. My supervisor, years back, she'd stand behind you with a clipboard counting. I told her where she could put her clipboard.
Tomasz: My checklist I fill in after, sometimes. So I'm not a good example.
Lorraine A: Nobody does them proper. Do you miss it, when you're at the uni? Being on your own, I mean.
Tomasz: Erm. Yeah, a bit. At uni everyone is nineteen and talks very fast and very sure. I sit at the back. I'm thirty-seven. My wife earns, you know, much more than me, she's pharmacist. So sometimes I think, what am I doing. And then I go to a museum and look at some old pot and I feel okay again. That's not very sensible, I know.
Lorraine A: No, it's sensible. Better than lying awake.
Tomasz: You lie awake?

calls.C0164:

calls.C0165:

Stone rows, long lines of stones going across the moor, sometimes hundreds of metres, and nobody really knows why. And hut circles, where people lived, you can still see the rings of the walls in the grass. And the old field boundaries, reaves, they cut right across the moor. When you understand what you're looking at, it's like the whole landscape is sort of a document. Most people walk past. I don't blame them, it's raining usually.
Craig: Stone rows, yeah. That's brilliant, actually. We ride past Castlerigg sometimes, up near Keswick, the stone circle, and I always think I should stop and actually look at it instead of just stopping for a flapjack.

calls.C0166:

calls.C0167:
Lorraine B: Hiya. Can you hear me okay?

Lorraine B: You do, don't you, with the uni.

Thousands of people, shovels, baskets. And there's another one near you, Wat's Dyke, older maybe, and people still argue about who built which and why. So when you walk on it you're standing on something somebody was told to build twelve hundred years ago. I find that... I don't know. Amazing. Sorry. I talk too much about dirt.

Lorraine B: That's nice. You keep doing that. I lost my mam three years ago, and I still pick the phone up sometimes to ring her. Silly, isn't it.
Tomasz: No. It's not silly.
Lorraine B: I don't know why I said that. Sorry.
Tomasz: It's fine. Really. What did she —
calls.C0168:
Craig: Hiya mate, can you hear me?

calls.C0169:
Colin: Hello, mate. Colin, down in Worthing. Can you hear me alright?
Tomasz: Yes. Hello, Colin. Tomasz, in Exeter.
Colin: Tomasz. Have I said that right?
Tomasz: Yes, perfect. Better than most people.
Colin: I did a bit of Spanish at evening class, so I'm very careful with names now. I saw your Dartmoor map in the picture. I put down you looked like a teacher.
Tomasz: Erm, no. Student. Archaeology, second year. And I work on a packing line, in a factory, nights and weekends.
Colin: Archaeology! Oh, I'm jealous now. I left school at sixteen, did my apprenticeship, never looked back. Except I did, later on. In lockdown I did an online course on the history of architecture, and I loved it more than anything I'd done in years. I thought, why didn't I do this at twenty?
Tomasz: I'm doing it at thirty-seven, so. Maybe it's never too late. Or maybe it is, I'll tell you in two years.
Colin: Ha. What got you into it, then?
Tomasz: Erm, it's a long answer. In Lublin there's the old town and a castle on the hill, and my grandmother used to take me round and tell me who was killed where, which for a child is very exciting. I started history at university there, then I left, came here for factory work, and I thought, okay, that's finished. Fifteen years. Then Hannah, my wife, she sort of pushed me to do the Access course at the college. And now I'm here.
Colin: That's not a long answer, that's a good answer.
Tomasz: Thank you. You were a builder?
Colin: Joiner. Kitchens, staircases, doors. My favourite was old sash windows, though, restoring them. You open one up and you can see how some bloke did it in eighteen-ninety, and he did it better than me, usually.
Tomasz: That's archaeology too, a bit. Reading a building.
Colin: Is it? I'll put it on my CV.
Tomasz: Really. In old buildings they look at how the timber was cut, the tool marks, and it helps to date it.
Colin: Tool marks, yeah. I did a job on a church roof once, years ago, and you could see the adze marks on the beams, every one a bit different. Somebody's whole week, that beam.
Tomasz: Mm. Somebody's whole life, maybe, that roof.
Colin: That's it. That's why I want to see Japan, the old wooden temples. Before the knees go.
Tomasz: Hannah wants Crete. Knossos. I want it too, but she wants the beach as well.
Colin: Oh, you can do both. We did Granada, the Alhambra. I've never seen anything like it. All that carved plaster, it's like lace.
Tomasz: When were you there?
Colin: Ooh, er, let me think. Twenty-twelve? Thirteen? Not the most organised with dates. We missed the train back to Málaga, I remember that.
Tomasz: I don't plan either. I book everything last minute. Hannah gets very angry.
Colin: Maureen too. Thirty-odd years she's been angry, and I've still not learnt.
Tomasz: Good. So there's no hope for me. That's relaxing.
Colin: Ha, none at all, mate. What are you reading at the minute, apart from all the uni stuff?
Tomasz: Lem, again. Polish science fiction. And a book about old field boundaries, which sounds boring, but it's not.
Colin: I'd read that. I've got three library books on the go and I'll finish one, if I'm lucky.
Tomasz: I have four. I think the library is worried about me.
Colin: They'll send someone round. What's the field boundary one, is it —
calls.C0170:

Lorraine B: There you go, then. Are you working, love?

Lorraine B: They don't, do they. You fill in all them pages and then nothing. It knocks you a bit.
Lorraine A: It does. I hate the forms. And the interview, sitting there with someone half your age asking where you see yourself in five years. I don't know. On me settee.

Lorraine A: I would. That's probably why they don't ring.
Lorraine B: Have you got kids?

Lorraine A: It's alright. Long story. ...Did you see Corrie last night?
Lorraine B: I did, yes. I couldn't believe it when she —
calls.C0171:

Lorraine A: Yeah. Lorraine. Wednesbury.
Tomasz: Tomasz. Exeter. You're the last one for me, I think.

calls.C0172:

C0169.line_text: Mm. Somebody's whole life, maybe, that roof.
C0169.what: At the right edge of the frame a T-shirt slips off the clothes airer behind Tomasz and drops out of view to the floor, with a faint soft thump on the mic; Tomasz doesn't turn round.
